claim: All cells have mechanisms to ensure degradation of partial proteins resulting from incomplete translation to safeguard proteome integrity.
source: When ribosomes fail to complete normal translation, all cells have mechanisms to ensure degradation of the resulting partial proteins to safeguard proteome integrity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cellular quality control mechanisms.

claim: In Escherichia coli and other eubacteria, the tmRNA system rescues stalled ribosomes.
source: In Escherichia coli and other eubacteria, the tmRNA system rescues stalled ribosomes and adds an ssrA tag or degron to the C-terminus of the incomplete protein, which directs degradation by the AAA+ ClpXP protease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial ribosome rescue systems.

claim: The tmRNA system adds an ssrA tag or degron to the C-terminus of incomplete proteins.
source: In Escherichia coli and other eubacteria, the tmRNA system rescues stalled ribosomes and adds an ssrA tag or degron to the C-terminus of the incomplete protein, which directs degradation by the AAA+ ClpXP protease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tmRNA tagging mechanism.

claim: The ssrA tag directs degradation by the AAA+ ClpXP protease.
source: In Escherichia coli and other eubacteria, the tmRNA system rescues stalled ribosomes and adds an ssrA tag or degron to the C-terminus of the incomplete protein, which directs degradation by the AAA+ ClpXP protease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the ssrA tag.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of ClpXP bound to the ssrA degron were obtained.
source: Here, we present cryo-EM structures of ClpXP bound to the ssrA degron.
evidence: The manuscript presents new structural data obtained through cryo-EM experiments.

claim: C-terminal residues of the ssrA degron initially bind in the top of an otherwise closed ClpX axial channel.
source: C-terminal residues of the ssrA degron initially bind in the top of an otherwise closed ClpX axial channel and subsequently move deeper into an open channel.
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ssrA degron subsequently moves deeper into an open ClpX channel.
source: C-terminal residues of the ssrA degron initially bind in the top of an otherwise closed ClpX axial channel and subsequently move deeper into an open channel.
evidence: This is a finding from the cryo-EM structures showing two different conformational states.

claim: Unfolding can occur directly from the initial closed-channel complex for short-degron protein substrates.
source: For short-degron protein substrates, we show that unfolding can occur directly from the initial closed-channel complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated through degradation assays with GFP substrates having different degron lengths.

claim: Many AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling motors are likely to employ similar multistep recognition and engagement strategies.
source: Many AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling motors are likely to employ similar multistep recognition and engagement strategies.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings about ClpXP mechanism.

claim: ClpX and/or ClpP are potential therapeutic targets for bacterial pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: ClpX (a AAA+ protein unfoldase/translocase) and/or ClpP (a self-compartmentalized peptidase) are also potential therapeutic targets for bacterial pathogens, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, as well as in human developmental defects, hematological disease, and cancer (Bhandari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ClpX and/or ClpP are potential therapeutic targets in human developmental defects, hematological disease, and cancer.
source: ClpX (a AAA+ protein unfoldase/translocase) and/or ClpP (a self-compartmentalized peptidase) are also potential therapeutic targets for bacterial pathogens, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, as well as in human developmental defects, hematological disease, and cancer (Bhandari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AAA+ proteases in bacteria and eukaryotic organelles typically recognize substrates via short N- or C-terminal peptide sequences.
source: In bacteria and eukaryotic organelles, AAA+ proteases typically recognize substrates via short N- or C-terminal peptide sequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AAA+ protease substrate recognition.

claim: Escherichia coli ClpXP degrades proteins bearing a C-terminal degron called the ssrA tag.
source: Escherichia coli ClpXP, for example, degrades proteins bearing a C-terminal degron called the ssrA tag that is added during tmRNA-rescue of stalled ribosomes (Keiler et al., 1996; Keiler, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ssrA tag is added during tmRNA-rescue of stalled ribosomes.
source: Escherichia coli ClpXP, for example, degrades proteins bearing a C-terminal degron called the ssrA tag that is added during tmRNA-rescue of stalled ribosomes (Keiler et al., 1996; Keiler, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During rescue, tmRNA binds in the empty A-site of a stalled ribosome.
source: During rescue, tmRNA binds in the empty A-site of a stalled ribosome, adds a charged alanine to the nascent polypeptide in a tRNA-like reaction, replaces the original mRNA with a short open reading frame that directs translation of the remaining residues of the ssrA degron, and finally recruits translation termination factors via a stop codon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tmRNA rescue mechanism.

claim: tmRNA adds a charged alanine to the nascent polypeptide in a tRNA-like reaction.
source: During rescue, tmRNA binds in the empty A-site of a stalled ribosome, adds a charged alanine to the nascent polypeptide in a tRNA-like reaction, replaces the original mRNA with a short open reading frame that directs translation of the remaining residues of the ssrA degron, and finally recruits translation termination factors via a stop codon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tmRNA rescue mechanism.

claim: tmRNA replaces the original mRNA with a short open reading frame that directs translation of the remaining residues of the ssrA degron.
source: During rescue, tmRNA binds in the empty A-site of a stalled ribosome, adds a charged alanine to the nascent polypeptide in a tRNA-like reaction, replaces the original mRNA with a short open reading frame that directs translation of the remaining residues of the ssrA degron, and finally recruits translation termination factors via a stop codon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tmRNA rescue mechanism.

claim: tmRNA recruits translation termination factors via a stop codon.
source: During rescue, tmRNA binds in the empty A-site of a stalled ribosome, adds a charged alanine to the nascent polypeptide in a tRNA-like reaction, replaces the original mRNA with a short open reading frame that directs translation of the remaining residues of the ssrA degron, and finally recruits translation termination factors via a stop codon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tmRNA rescue mechanism.

claim: A different bacterial mechanism adds alanine tails to the nascent polypeptide during the ribosome-rescue reaction.
source: A different bacterial mechanism, which is similar to eukaryotic systems, adds alanine tails to the nascent polypeptide during the ribosome-rescue reaction (Buskirk and Green, 2017; Lytvynenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The sequence of the E. coli ssrA tag is AANDENYALAA-coo–.
source: The sequence of the E. coli ssrA tag is AANDENYALAA-coo– (Keiler et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The terminal Ala-Ala-coo– dipeptide of the ssrA degron is the most important element for ClpXP degradation.
source: The terminal Ala-Ala-coo– dipeptide of this degron is the most important element for ClpXP degradation (Flynn et al., 2001), and related degrons ending in Ala-Ala target other cellular proteins to ClpXP (Flynn et al., 2003; Neher et al., 2006; Lytvynenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Related degrons ending in Ala-Ala target other cellular proteins to ClpXP.
source: The terminal Ala-Ala-coo– dipeptide of this degron is the most important element for ClpXP degradation (Flynn et al., 2001), and related degrons ending in Ala-Ala target other cellular proteins to ClpXP (Flynn et al., 2003; Neher et al., 2006; Lytvynenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ssrA tag initially binds in the axial channel of the hexameric AAA+ ClpX ring.
source: The ssrA tag initially binds in the axial channel of the hexameric AAA+ ClpX ring, where the pore-1, pore-2, and RKH loops contribute to recognition (Siddiqui et al., 2004; Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008b; Iosefson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pore-1, pore-2, and RKH loops of ClpX contribute to ssrA tag recognition.
source: The ssrA tag initially binds in the axial channel of the hexameric AAA+ ClpX ring, where the pore-1, pore-2, and RKH loops contribute to recognition (Siddiqui et al., 2004; Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008b; Iosefson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Subsequent mechanical reactions requiring ATP hydrolysis unfold adjacent regions of native protein structure.
source: Subsequent mechanical reactions requiring ATP hydrolysis unfold adjacent regions of native protein structure and then translocate the denatured polypeptide through the channel and into the degradation chamber of the double-ring ClpP14 peptidase for proteolysis (Sauer and Baker, 2011; Olivares et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ClpXP translocates the denatured polypeptide through the channel and into the degradation chamber of the double-ring ClpP14 peptidase for proteolysis.
source: Subsequent mechanical reactions requiring ATP hydrolysis unfold adjacent regions of native protein structure and then translocate the denatured polypeptide through the channel and into the degradation chamber of the double-ring ClpP14 peptidase for proteolysis (Sauer and Baker, 2011; Olivares et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Classification and three-dimensional reconstruction of EM images generated density maps at resolutions of 3.1–3.2 Å.
source: Classification and three-dimensional reconstruction of EM images containing one ClpX∆N pseudohexamer and one ClpP tetradecamer generated density maps of ClpX bound to one heptameric ring of ClpP14 and 7–10 residues of the ssrA degron in two distinct conformations at resolutions of 3.1–3.2 Å (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the cryo-EM data collection and processing.

claim: Two distinct conformations of ClpX bound to the ssrA degron were observed.
source: Classification and three-dimensional reconstruction of EM images containing one ClpX∆N pseudohexamer and one ClpP tetradecamer generated density maps of ClpX bound to one heptameric ring of ClpP14 and 7–10 residues of the ssrA degron in two distinct conformations at resolutions of 3.1–3.2 Å (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the cryo-EM data collection and processing.

claim: Subunits of the ClpX∆N hexamer formed a shallow spiral.
source: As seen in previous high-resolution cryo-EM structures (Fei et al., 2020; Ripstein et al., 2020), subunits of the ClpX∆N hexamer formed a shallow spiral (labeled ABCDEF from the top to the bottom of the spiral in the clockwise direction), which docked asymmetrically with a flat ClpP7 ring.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, consistent with prior structures.

claim: The ClpX hexamer docked asymmetrically with a flat ClpP7 ring.
source: As seen in previous high-resolution cryo-EM structures (Fei et al., 2020; Ripstein et al., 2020), subunits of the ClpX∆N hexamer formed a shallow spiral (labeled ABCDEF from the top to the bottom of the spiral in the clockwise direction), which docked asymmetrically with a flat ClpP7 ring.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, consistent with prior structures.

claim: The pore of the cis ClpP ring contacting ClpX was open.
source: The pore of the cis ClpP ring contacting ClpX was open, as expected (Fei et al., 2020; Ripstein et al., 2020), but the pore of the trans ClpP ring was closed in both new structures.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, consistent with prior structures.

claim: The pore of the trans ClpP ring was closed in both new structures.
source: The pore of the cis ClpP ring contacting ClpX was open, as expected (Fei et al., 2020; Ripstein et al., 2020), but the pore of the trans ClpP ring was closed in both new structures.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The ssrA degron moved ~25 Å or six residues deeper into the channel between the recognition complex and intermediate complex.
source: The ssrA degron bound in the top of the ClpX channel in a structure we call the recognition complex and moved ~25 Å or six residues deeper into the channel in a structure we call the intermediate complex (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two cryo-EM structures.

claim: The presence of clear side-chain density for the ssrA degron is the most important difference between the current structures and those previously reported.
source: The presence of clear side-chain density for the ssrA degron is the most important difference between our current structures and those previously reported by our group (Fei et al., 2020) and by Ripstein et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior structural studies.

claim: In previous structures by Fei et al., uncharacterized substrates apparently copurified with ClpXP.
source: By contrast, in our previous structures, uncharacterized substrates apparently copurified with ClpXP, whereas a specific substrate was used for the studies of Ripstein et al. but no side-chain density was observed.
evidence: This is an inference about prior structural studies.

claim: In the studies of Ripstein et al., a specific substrate was used but no side-chain density was observed.
source: By contrast, in our previous structures, uncharacterized substrates apparently copurified with ClpXP, whereas a specific substrate was used for the studies of Ripstein et al. but no side-chain density was observed.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior structural studies.

claim: The ssrA degron was contacted by the RKH, pore-1, and pore-2 loops of ClpX in the recognition complex.
source: The ssrA degron bound high in the axial channel of the recognition complex, where it was contacted by the RKH, pore-1, and pore-2 loops of ClpX (Figures 1B and 2A–2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Access to the lower channel in the recognition complex was blocked by a previously unvisualized conformation of the pore-2 loop of ClpX subunit A.
source: Importantly, access to the lower channel in this recognition complex was blocked by a previously unvisualized conformation of the pore-2 loop of ClpX subunit A (Figures 1B, 2B, C and D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Blockage of the axial pore has not been observed in other structures of ClpXP or different AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines.
source: Blockage of the axial pore has not been observed in other structures of ClpXP or different AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior structural studies of AAA+ machines.

claim: Thr199 and Val202 side chains from the blocking pore-2 loop made van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions with the Cβ methyl of the C-terminal alanine of the ssrA degron.
source: Thr199 and Val202 side chains from the blocking pore-2 loop in the recognition complex made van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions with the Cβ methyl of the C-terminal alanine of the ssrA degron, and the side chain –OH of the same Thr199 side chain as well as the peptide –NH of Val154 in the pore-1 loop of chain B made hydrogen bonds with the α-coo– of the ssrA degron (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The side chain –OH of Thr199 and the peptide –NH of Val154 made hydrogen bonds with the α-coo– of the ssrA degron.
source: Thr199 and Val202 side chains from the blocking pore-2 loop in the recognition complex made van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions with the Cβ methyl of the C-terminal alanine of the ssrA degron, and the side chain –OH of the same Thr199 side chain as well as the peptide –NH of Val154 in the pore-1 loop of chain B made hydrogen bonds with the α-coo– of the ssrA degron (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Tyr153 and Val154 side-chain or main-chain groups from pore-1 loops made additional contacts with the Ala-Ala-coo– or neighboring degron regions.
source: Tyr153 and Val154 side-chain or main-chain groups from pore-1 loops (subunits A/B) or Arg228 and His230 side chains from RKH loops (subunits B/C/D/F) made additional contacts with the Ala-Ala-coo– or neighboring degron regions (Figure 2C, D and E; Video 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Arg228 and His230 side chains from RKH loops made additional contacts with the Ala-Ala-coo– or neighboring degron regions.
source: Tyr153 and Val154 side-chain or main-chain groups from pore-1 loops (subunits A/B) or Arg228 and His230 side chains from RKH loops (subunits B/C/D/F) made additional contacts with the Ala-Ala-coo– or neighboring degron regions (Figure 2C, D and E; Video 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Mutation of the penultimate or ultimate C-terminal alanines of the ssrA tag in 29-residue peptide substrates increased KM for ClpXP degradation.
source: First, as expected based upon the recognition-complex structure (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), we found that mutation of the penultimate or ultimate C-terminal alanines of the ssrA tag in 29-residue peptide substrates increased KM for ClpXP degradation but had little effect on Vmax (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from degradation assays with mutant peptides.

claim: Mutation of the penultimate or ultimate C-terminal alanines of the ssrA tag had little effect on Vmax.
source: First, as expected based upon the recognition-complex structure (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), we found that mutation of the penultimate or ultimate C-terminal alanines of the ssrA tag in 29-residue peptide substrates increased KM for ClpXP degradation but had little effect on Vmax (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from degradation assays with mutant peptides.

claim: Mutation of the antepenultimate residue of the ssrA tag (leucine) increases KM modestly.
source: A prior study showed that mutation of the antepenultimate residue of the ssrA tag (leucine) or the amino acid two residues upstream (tyrosine) also increases KM modestly (Flynn et al., 2001), which can also be rationalized based upon recognition-complex contacts (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mutation of the amino acid two residues upstream of the C-terminus (tyrosine) increases KM modestly.
source: A prior study showed that mutation of the antepenultimate residue of the ssrA tag (leucine) or the amino acid two residues upstream (tyrosine) also increases KM modestly (Flynn et al., 2001), which can also be rationalized based upon recognition-complex contacts (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Y153A, V154F, and R228A ClpX mutations increase KM for ClpP degradation of ssrA-tagged substrates 50-fold or more.
source: Second, previously characterized Y153A, V154F, and R228A ClpX mutations increase KM for ClpP degradation of ssrA-tagged substrates 50-fold or more (Siddiqui et al., 2004; Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008b; Iosefson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The T199A, T199V, V202A, and H230A mutations caused large increases in KM for GFP-ssrA degradation.
source: In assays of GFP-ssrA degradation, the T199A, T199V, V202A, and H230A mutations caused large increases in KM (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from degradation assays with ClpX mutants.

claim: KM for degradation by the T199S variant increased only ~4-fold.
source: By contrast, KM for degradation by the conservative T199S variant increased only ~4-fold (Figure 3A), supporting a key role for a hydrogen bond between the side-chain hydroxyl of Thr199 in ClpX and the α-carboxylate of the ssrA degron (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a result from degradation assays with a ClpX mutant.

claim: The R228A variant displays reduced specificity for an ssrA-tagged substrate and increased specificity for an N-degron substrate compared to wild-type ClpXP.
source: Third, compared to wild-type ClpXP, the R228A variant displays reduced specificity for an ssrA-tagged substrate and increased specificity for an N-degron substrate (Farrell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Human ClpXP has leucines at positions corresponding to Thr199 and His230 in E. coli ClpX.
source: Finally, human ClpXP has leucines at positions corresponding to Thr199 and His230 in E. coli ClpX and does not degrade ssrA-tagged substrates, but a human hybrid containing transplanted pore-2 and RKH loops from the E. coli enzyme acquires this activity (Martin et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Human ClpXP does not degrade ssrA-tagged substrates.
source: Finally, human ClpXP has leucines at positions corresponding to Thr199 and His230 in E. coli ClpX and does not degrade ssrA-tagged substrates, but a human hybrid containing transplanted pore-2 and RKH loops from the E. coli enzyme acquires this activity (Martin et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A human ClpXP hybrid containing transplanted pore-2 and RKH loops from the E. coli enzyme acquires the activity to degrade ssrA-tagged substrates.
source: Finally, human ClpXP has leucines at positions corresponding to Thr199 and His230 in E. coli ClpX and does not degrade ssrA-tagged substrates, but a human hybrid containing transplanted pore-2 and RKH loops from the E. coli enzyme acquires this activity (Martin et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the intermediate complex, five ClpX pore-1 loops and four pore-2 loops packed against degron side chains with a periodicity of two residues.
source: In the intermediate complex, five ClpX pore-1 loops and four pore-2 loops packed against degron side chains with a periodicity of two residues (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D, Video 2).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The arrangement of pore loops interacting with polypeptide in the channel has been observed previously in ClpXP complexes with other substrates and in different AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines.
source: This arrangement of pore loops interacting with polypeptide in the channel has been observed previously in ClpXP complexes with other substrates and in different AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines (Fei et al., 2020; Ripstein et al., 2020; Puchades et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: These enzyme structures are thought to reflect snapshots during non-specific translocation.
source: These enzyme structures are thought to reflect snapshots during non-specific translocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations and prior knowledge.

claim: ClpXP translocates a variety of sequences, including polymeric tracts of glycine, proline, lysine, arginine, glutamate, and glutamine.
source: Indeed, ClpXP translocates a variety of sequences, including polymeric tracts of glycine, proline, lysine, arginine, glutamate, and glutamine (Barkow et al., 2009), and the specific contacts observed in the recognition complex were absent in the intermediate complex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The specific contacts observed in the recognition complex were absent in the intermediate complex.
source: Indeed, ClpXP translocates a variety of sequences, including polymeric tracts of glycine, proline, lysine, arginine, glutamate, and glutamine (Barkow et al., 2009), and the specific contacts observed in the recognition complex were absent in the intermediate complex.
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two cryo-EM structures.

claim: Non-specific translocation allows ClpXP to degrade any protein after degron recognition and unfolding of attached native structure.
source: Non-specific translocation allows ClpXP to degrade any protein after degron recognition and unfolding of attached native structure (Sauer and Baker, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The pore-2 loop of ClpX subunit A occludes the axial channel prior to substrate binding.
source: By contrast, our results suggest that the pore-2 loop of ClpX subunit A occludes the axial channel (Figure 2B) prior to substrate binding, thereby preventing non-specific binding and degron-independent degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Occlusion of the axial channel prevents non-specific binding and degron-independent degradation.
source: By contrast, our results suggest that the pore-2 loop of ClpX subunit A occludes the axial channel (Figure 2B) prior to substrate binding, thereby preventing non-specific binding and degron-independent degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: A recent study of the kinetics of ClpXP association with a substrate bearing a 20-residue ssrA degron provides evidence for three sequentially occupied substrate-bound conformations.
source: However, a recent study of the kinetics of ClpXP association with a substrate bearing a 20-residue ssrA degron similar to the one studied here provides evidence for three sequentially occupied substrate-bound conformations (Saunders et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The first two kinetically defined states likely correspond to the recognition and intermediate complexes.
source: The first two are likely to correspond to our recognition and intermediate complexes.
evidence: This is an inference connecting kinetic data from prior work to the structural observations.

claim: Conversion of the first to the second complex depends on the rate of ATP hydrolysis.
source: Conversion of the first to the second complex depends on the rate of ATP hydrolysis, as does formation of the third kinetically defined state, which is probably similar to the fully engaged complex depicted in Figure 5.
evidence: This is an inference based on kinetic data from prior work.

claim: Formation of the third kinetically defined state depends on the rate of ATP hydrolysis.
source: Conversion of the first to the second complex depends on the rate of ATP hydrolysis, as does formation of the third kinetically defined state, which is probably similar to the fully engaged complex depicted in Figure 5.
evidence: This is an inference based on kinetic data from prior work.

claim: The third kinetically defined state is probably similar to the fully engaged complex.
source: Conversion of the first to the second complex depends on the rate of ATP hydrolysis, as does formation of the third kinetically defined state, which is probably similar to the fully engaged complex depicted in Figure 5.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting kinetic data to structural models.

claim: Prior ClpXP complexes show the native portion of a protein substrate contacting the top of the central channel with an attached peptide filling the channel.
source: Prior ClpXP complexes showing the native portion of a protein substrate contacting the top of the central channel with an attached peptide filling the channel (Fei et al., 2020) provide structural evidence for this fully engaged state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ClpX can unfold short-degron substrates directly from the closed-channel recognition complex.
source: Our results indicate that ClpX can unfold short-degron substrates directly from the closed-channel recognition complex, in which just two pore-1 loops contact the degron, and long-degron substrates from a subsequent open-channel engaged complex in which five pore-1 loops engage the substrate (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the degradation assays with different degron lengths.

claim: In the recognition complex, just two pore-1 loops contact the degron.
source: Our results indicate that ClpX can unfold short-degron substrates directly from the closed-channel recognition complex, in which just two pore-1 loops contact the degron, and long-degron substrates from a subsequent open-channel engaged complex in which five pore-1 loops engage the substrate (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: ClpX unfolds long-degron substrates from a subsequent open-channel engaged complex in which five pore-1 loops engage the substrate.
source: Our results indicate that ClpX can unfold short-degron substrates directly from the closed-channel recognition complex, in which just two pore-1 loops contact the degron, and long-degron substrates from a subsequent open-channel engaged complex in which five pore-1 loops engage the substrate (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Substrate residues in the upper part of the channel are gripped most tightly during ClpXP unfolding of substrates with long degrons.
source: Although unfolding in these two cases must be somewhat different in terms of the detailed mechanism, substrate residues in the upper part of the channel are gripped most tightly during ClpXP unfolding of substrates with long degrons (Bell et al., 2019), supporting a model in which ClpX-substrate contacts near the top of the channel play key roles in both unfolding mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ClpX-substrate contacts near the top of the channel play key roles in both unfolding mechanisms.
source: Although unfolding in these two cases must be somewhat different in terms of the detailed mechanism, substrate residues in the upper part of the channel are gripped most tightly during ClpXP unfolding of substrates with long degrons (Bell et al., 2019), supporting a model in which ClpX-substrate contacts near the top of the channel play key roles in both unfolding mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work and the current structural data.

claim: The multistep mechanism for protein degradation by ClpXP may be used by related AAA+ proteases that recognize unstructured degrons.
source: The multistep mechanism proposed here for protein degradation by ClpXP may be used by related AAA+ proteases that recognize unstructured degrons, as it nicely resolves how unfolding motors make initiation highly specific (and thus limited to appropriate protein targets) but then allow nonspecific unfolding and translocation for subsequent degradation and/or remodeling.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the generality of the mechanism.

claim: The multistep mechanism resolves how unfolding motors make initiation highly specific but then allow nonspecific unfolding and translocation.
source: The multistep mechanism proposed here for protein degradation by ClpXP may be used by related AAA+ proteases that recognize unstructured degrons, as it nicely resolves how unfolding motors make initiation highly specific (and thus limited to appropriate protein targets) but then allow nonspecific unfolding and translocation for subsequent degradation and/or remodeling.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the mechanism.

claim: AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines must deal with problems similar to those encountered by multisubunit enzymes in transcription, translation, DNA replication, and protein secretion.
source: More generally, AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines must deal with problems similar to those encountered by multisubunit enzymes in transcription, translation, DNA replication, and protein secretion, which also require transitions from specific recognition conformations to complexes that utilize the chemical energy of ATP or GTP hydrolysis to processively and non-specifically move along their polymeric substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison with other molecular machines.

claim: Multisubunit enzymes in transcription, translation, DNA replication, and protein secretion require transitions from specific recognition conformations to complexes that processively and non-specifically move along their polymeric substrates.
source: More generally, AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines must deal with problems similar to those encountered by multisubunit enzymes in transcription, translation, DNA replication, and protein secretion, which also require transitions from specific recognition conformations to complexes that utilize the chemical energy of ATP or GTP hydrolysis to processively and non-specifically move along their polymeric substrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about molecular machines.

claim: GFP-laa was not degraded by ClpXP.
source: Strikingly, GFP-laa was not degraded, whereas GFP-yalaa and substrates with longer tags were robustly degraded (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from degradation assays with different GFP substrates.

claim: GFP-yalaa and substrates with longer tags were robustly degraded by ClpXP.
source: Strikingly, GFP-laa was not degraded, whereas GFP-yalaa and substrates with longer tags were robustly degraded (Figure 4B).

claim: The native barrel of GFP-yalaa docked snugly with the top of the AAA+ ClpX ring, with the yalaa in the same position as in the recognition complex.
source: Modeling revealed that the native barrel of GFP-yalaa docked snugly with the top of the AAA+ ClpX ring, with the yalaa in the same position as in the recognition complex (Figure 4C and D; Video 3).
evidence: This is a result from molecular modeling based on the cryo-EM structure.

source: By contrast, the tag of GFP-laa was too short to allow formation of recognition-complex contacts without severe steric clashes with ClpX.
evidence: This is an inference from molecular modeling.

claim: The inability of ClpXP to degrade GFP-laa argues against a model for degradation in which the C-terminal β-strand of GFP spontaneously denatures.
source: The inability of ClpXP to degrade GFP-laa also argues against a model for degradation in which the C-terminal β-strand of GFP spontaneously denatures.

claim: A power stroke initiated directly from the recognition complex can unfold GFP-yalaa.
source: We conclude that a power stroke initiated directly from the recognition complex can unfold GFP-yalaa (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the degradation assays and structural data.

claim: Subunits ABCDE of ClpX contained ATP/ATPγS and subunit F contained ADP in the recognition complex.
source: Subunits ABCDE of ClpX contained ATP/ATPγS and subunit F contained ADP in the recognition complex, whereas subunit A was nucleotide free and the remaining subunits were ATP/ATPγS bound in the intermediate complex (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Subunit A was nucleotide free and the remaining subunits were ATP/ATPγS bound in the intermediate complex.
source: Subunits ABCDE of ClpX contained ATP/ATPγS and subunit F contained ADP in the recognition complex, whereas subunit A was nucleotide free and the remaining subunits were ATP/ATPγS bound in the intermediate complex (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: ATP hydrolysis in subunit A of the recognition complex drives an unfolding power stroke and conversion to the intermediate complex.
source: Thus, it is plausible that ATP hydrolysis in subunit A of the recognition complex drives an unfolding power stroke and conversion to the intermediate complex.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the nucleotide states observed in the structures.

claim: The six-residue offset in the position of the ssrA tag between the two complexes is consistent with optical-trap experiments that show a fundamental ClpXP translocation step of 5–8 amino acids.
source: The six-residue offset in the position of the ssrA tag between the two complexes (Figure 1B) is consistent with optical-trap experiments that show a fundamental ClpXP translocation step of 5–8 amino acids (Aubin-Tam et al., 2011; Maillard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior experimental work.

claim: For sufficiently short tags, a single power stroke from the recognition complex could move the tag six residues deeper into the channel, unfolding native structure N-terminal to the tag in the process.
source: Hence, for sufficiently short tags, a single power stroke from the recognition complex could move the tag six residues deeper into the channel, unfolding native structure N-terminal to the tag in the process (Figures 4E and 5, bottom pathway).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: For longer tags, continued translocation after the first power stroke would eventually bring the native protein in contact with the top of the ClpX channel, where additional power strokes could apply an unfolding force.
source: For longer tags, including the 20-residue degron used for our cryo-EM studies, continued translocation after the first power stroke would eventually bring the native protein in contact with the top of the ClpX channel, where additional power strokes could apply an unfolding force (Figure 5, top pathway).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The recognition complex of ClpX bound to the ssrA degron is unique compared to previously determined structures.
source: Strikingly, the recognition complex of ClpX bound to the ssrA degron is unique compared to previously determined structures.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior structural studies.

claim: All previous ClpXP structures have open channels.
source: For example, all previous structures have open channels, whereas the axial channel of the AAA+ ring of ClpX in the recognition complex is closed by the pore-2 loop of subunit A, which makes specific contacts with the C-terminal residue of the ssrA tag.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior structural studies.

claim: Only the pore-1 loops of the top two subunits in the ClpX spiral contact the substrate degron in the recognition complex.
source: Moreover, only the pore-1 loops of the top two subunits in the ClpX spiral contact the substrate degron in the recognition complex, as opposed to contacts between five pore-1 loops and substrates in other known structures.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: In other known ClpXP structures, five pore-1 loops contact substrates.
source: Moreover, only the pore-1 loops of the top two subunits in the ClpX spiral contact the substrate degron in the recognition complex, as opposed to contacts between five pore-1 loops and substrates in other known structures.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior structural studies.

claim: The contacts between ClpX and the ssrA degron in the recognition complex explain why the C-terminal Ala-Ala dipeptide of the ssrA tag is most important for ClpXP degradation.
source: The contacts we see between ClpX and the ssrA degron in the recognition complex explain multiple biochemical results, including ones that show that the C-terminal Ala-Ala dipeptide of the ssrA tag is most important for ClpXP degradation (Flynn et al., 2001; Figure 3A) and others that demonstrate that the side chains of six ClpX residues in the pore-1 loop (Tyr153, Val154), pore-2 loop (Thr199, Val202), and RKH loop (Arg228, His230) play critical roles both in substrate binding and in substrate specificity (Siddiqui et al., 2004; Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008b; Iosefson et al., 2015; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural observations to prior biochemical data.

claim: The contacts between ClpX and the ssrA degron in the recognition complex explain why the side chains of six ClpX residues play critical roles in substrate binding and substrate specificity.
source: The contacts we see between ClpX and the ssrA degron in the recognition complex explain multiple biochemical results, including ones that show that the C-terminal Ala-Ala dipeptide of the ssrA tag is most important for ClpXP degradation (Flynn et al., 2001; Figure 3A) and others that demonstrate that the side chains of six ClpX residues in the pore-1 loop (Tyr153, Val154), pore-2 loop (Thr199, Val202), and RKH loop (Arg228, His230) play critical roles both in substrate binding and in substrate specificity (Siddiqui et al., 2004; Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008b; Iosefson et al., 2015; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural observations to prior biochemical data.

claim: The closed axial channel of the recognition complex would preclude the non-specific binding of substrate polypeptides that is observed in the open channels of the intermediate complex and related structures.
source: In addition to providing a specific binding site for the ssrA degron, the closed axial channel of the recognition complex would preclude the non-specific binding of substrate polypeptides that is observed in the open channels of the intermediate complex and related structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Non-specific binding in the intermediate complex explains how ClpXP efficiently translocates and degrades diverse polypeptide sequences.
source: Non-specific binding in the intermediate complex explains how ClpXP efficiently translocates and degrades diverse polypeptide sequences (Barkow et al., 2009), including unnatural amino acids, but could also result in inappropriate degradation of proteins that initially bound in an open channel.
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural observations to prior biochemical data.

claim: Non-specific binding in an open channel could result in inappropriate degradation of proteins.
source: Non-specific binding in the intermediate complex explains how ClpXP efficiently translocates and degrades diverse polypeptide sequences (Barkow et al., 2009), including unnatural amino acids, but could also result in inappropriate degradation of proteins that initially bound in an open channel.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about potential problems with non-specific binding.

claim: Only following specific recognition of the ssrA degron in the closed-pore conformation does the pore-2 loop of subunit A move to permit passage and interaction of deeper channel residues with any polypeptide sequence.
source: Our structures suggest a simple solution to this problem. Only following specific recognition of the ssrA degron in the closed-pore conformation does the pore-2 loop of subunit A move to permit passage and interaction of deeper channel residues with any polypeptide sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: An ATPγS/ATP mixture was used to allow rapid substrate binding, while slowing translocation and unfolding.
source: An ATPγS/ATP mixture was used to allow rapid substrate binding, while slowing translocation and unfolding (Burton et al., 2003; Martin et al., 2008a; Saunders et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citations to prior work.

claim: EM images contained complexes in which ClpP14 was bound to one (~60%) or two (~40%) ClpX∆N hexamers.
source: EM images contained complexes in which ClpP14 was bound to one (~60%) or two (~40%) ClpX∆N hexamers.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data collection.

claim: The recognition and intermediate complexes accounted for 92% of all of the singly capped complexes.
source: The recognition and intermediate complexes accounted for 92% of all of the singly capped complexes.
evidence: This is a result from the cryo-EM data processing and classification.

claim: ClpX hydrolyzes ATPγS more slowly than ATP.
source: Approximately 15 s before vitrification, we combined the GFP substrate and ATP with a mixture of the ClpX∆N variant, ClpP14, and ATPγS, which ClpX hydrolyzes more slowly than ATP (Burton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The general properties of the intermediate complex are similar to previously determined structures of ClpXP translocation complexes.
source: The general properties of the intermediate complex are similar to previously determined structures of ClpXP translocation complexes in the sense that the axial channel is open and five pore-1 loops and multiple pore-2 loops contact every two residues of the substrate polypeptide in the channel (Fei et al., 2020; Ripstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior structural studies.

claim: The structural feature of pore loops contacting every two residues of substrate has been widely observed in AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines.
source: This structural feature has been widely observed in AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines, suggesting that these diverse molecular machines employ a common mechanism of substrate translocation (for review, see Puchades et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Diverse AAA+ molecular machines employ a common mechanism of substrate translocation.
source: This structural feature has been widely observed in AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines, suggesting that these diverse molecular machines employ a common mechanism of substrate translocation (for review, see Puchades et al., 2020).
